html:
"Arctic marine mammal hunters" is the map's label for the peoples of the North American Arctic coasts, from Alaska to Greenland, who lived by hunting seals, walrus and whales. The map shows them from 2000 BCE to 1200 CE.

Almost nothing grows on the tundra, so food came from the sea and the herds. Hunters waited at seal breathing holes in the winter ice, took walrus and whales from boats, and hunted caribou, fish and birds in summer. Their key tools were the toggling harpoon, whose head turns sideways inside the animal, skin boats, and stone lamps that burned seal fat for heat and light.

Several cultures followed one another under this label:

  • The Paleo-Inuit spread east from Alaska around 2500 BCE with tiny, finely made stone blades, and reached Greenland, where the Saqqaq culture lived.
  • The Dorset culture held the eastern Arctic from about 500 BCE. Its people carved small ivory figures and did not use bows or dog sleds.
  • Around the Bering Strait, peoples developed open-water whaling with large skin boats.
  • From about 1000 CE the Thule people, ancestors of the Inuit, moved fast east from Alaska with dog sleds, kayaks and whaling gear, in the Thule migration. Within a few centuries they had replaced the Dorset.

This way of life, built on deep knowledge of ice, weather and animals, carried on into modern times among the Inuit and Yupik peoples.
sum: "Arctic marine mammal hunters" is the map's label for the peoples of the North American Arctic coasts, from Alaska to Greenland, who lived by hunting seals, walrus and whales. The map shows them from 2000 BCE to 1200 CE.
